steps.title: Прошлое, которого не было
steps.html:

steps.title: Три типа условия рядом
steps.html:
ТипЧасть с ifРезультат
Реальное (первое) — может произойтиif + present simplewill / may / can
Нереальное (второе) — сейчас, не такif + past simplewould / might / could
Нереальное прошлое (третье) — уже поздноif + past perfectwould / might / could + have + past participle
ПримерIf he had crashed into a town,he would have killed people.
ОтрицаниеIf he hadn't taught himself to fly,none of it would have happened.

steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Обе части — противоположность реальности. Он не разбился. Никто не погиб. → If he had crashed, he would have killed people.

might have и could have смягчают результат: he might have killed someone — менее уверенно, чем would have.

В части с if — никакого would. If I would have known — ошибка, правильно If I had known.

В формальном стиле if опускается, а had выходит вперёд: Had I known, I would have said something.

steps.title: The last outlaw
steps.html:
For two years a teenager stole planes, boats and cars across North America, and thousands of strangers cheered him on. Almost nobody asked what the people he robbed thought about it.

A  The police called him a suspect in more than a hundred thefts. The internet called him the barefoot bandit, because he often carried out his robberies with no shoes on, and because a photograph of bare footprints on a stolen floor is a better story than a list of charges. A Facebook page collecting support for him gathered tens of thousands of likes. Somebody wrote a song. He was nineteen, and he had reportedly taught himself to fly using information he found online.

B  The flying is what turned a local crime story into an international one. Between 2008 and 2010 he took at least five light aircraft, none of which he had ever been trained to operate, and crash-landed every one. He was finally captured in the Bahamas after flying a stolen plane more than a thousand miles from Indiana, running it out of fuel, and putting it down in shallow water. None of his victims were injured. That fact did a great deal of work in the way the story was told.

C  It is not difficult to see why people enjoyed it. The story had a shape that audiences already knew: a young man alone, technically skilled, taking from people who could afford the loss and hurting nobody. If he had used violence even once, the Facebook page would have emptied overnight. If anyone had been hurt in one of those landings, there would have been no song.

D  The people he stole from tell it differently. He did not only take aircraft. He broke into houses and small businesses in a rural area where a stolen boat is somebody’s income and an insurance claim takes months. One shop owner described lying awake listening to noises for a year afterwards. “They made him into a film,” she said. “Nobody made a film about the year I spent frightened in my own house.”

E  The court took a view somewhere between the two. He was sentenced to seven years, and the judge accepted that a childhood of extraordinary neglect was part of the explanation, though not an excuse. An unusual condition was attached to the sentence: any money made from the film rights would go straight to his victims. It was an attempt to correct, in a small way, the thing the case had exposed — that the story was worth far more than the damage was.

F  Perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not about him at all. If the same teenager had broken into the same houses without ever getting into a plane, nobody outside the county would have heard his name. He would have been an ordinary burglar with a difficult history, and he would have served his sentence unnoticed. The flying did not change what he took. It changed who was willing to watch.

Written for this course. Based on contemporary court reporting and published accounts of the case of Colton Harris-Moore (2008–2010).

steps.html:
The last outlaw

For two years a teenager stole planes, boats and cars across North America, and thousands of strangers cheered him on. Almost nobody asked what the people he robbed thought about it.

A  The police called him a suspect in more than a hundred thefts. The internet called him the barefoot bandit, because he often carried out his robberies with no shoes on, and because a photograph of bare footprints on a stolen floor is a better story than a list of charges. A Facebook page collecting support for him gathered tens of thousands of likes. Somebody wrote a song. He was nineteen, and he had reportedly taught himself to fly using information he found online.

B  The flying is what turned a local crime story into an international one. Between 2008 and 2010 he took at least five light aircraft, none of which he had ever been trained to operate, and crash-landed every one. He was finally captured in the Bahamas after flying a stolen plane more than a thousand miles from Indiana, running it out of fuel, and putting it down in shallow water. None of his victims were injured. That fact did a great deal of work in the way the story was told.

C  It is not difficult to see why people enjoyed it. The story had a shape that audiences already knew: a young man alone, technically skilled, taking from people who could afford the loss and hurting nobody. If he had used violence even once, the Facebook page would have emptied overnight. If anyone had been hurt in one of those landings, there would have been no song.

D  The people he stole from tell it differently. He did not only take aircraft. He broke into houses and small businesses in a rural area where a stolen boat is somebody’s income and an insurance claim takes months. One shop owner described lying awake listening to noises for a year afterwards. “They made him into a film,” she said. “Nobody made a film about the year I spent frightened in my own house.”

E  The court took a view somewhere between the two. He was sentenced to seven years, and the judge accepted that a childhood of extraordinary neglect was part of the explanation, though not an excuse. An unusual condition was attached to the sentence: any money made from the film rights would go straight to his victims. It was an attempt to correct, in a small way, the thing the case had exposed — that the story was worth far more than the damage was.

F  Perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not about him at all. If the same teenager had broken into the same houses without ever getting into a plane, nobody outside the county would have heard his name. He would have been an ordinary burglar with a difficult history, and he would have served his sentence unnoticed. The flying did not change what he took. It changed who was willing to watch.
